clue.text: Most distant meteors stray close to planet

indicators.note: to stray is to wander off course, so the letters of meteors wander into a new order
the close of a word is its end, so this takes the final letter of planet

explanation.surface: An astronomer notes the farthest-flung meteors drifting near a planet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stray' rearranges METEORS to REMOTES; 'close to' adds the T that ends 'planet'.
explanation.definitionFit: Remote means far away, so the superlative form is a straight synonym for farthest off.

clue.text: Sweet that's not crammed with unlimited sugar

indicators.note: something crammed with a filling has it packed inside, so the word not is stuffed with other letters
without its limits, the word sugar loses its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A confection is described as one not packed with sugar.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is ironic, since this confection is packed full of sugar; 'crammed with' and 'unlimited' are the indicators.
explanation.definitionFit: Nougat is a chewy confection of sugar or honey with nuts, a classic sweet.

clue.text: Food outlet very nearly is screening key Labour results?

parts.note: a deli is a delicatessen, a shop selling prepared food

indicators.note: nearly the whole word, so very loses its last letter

parts.note: taken as written before trimming

indicators.note: to screen is to shield or hide, so the word is wraps around another letter

parts.note: taken as written
E is a musical key

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a food shop's output reflects the Labour Party's results.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' is not the political party: it is childbirth, whose results are babies delivered. 'nearly' and 'screening' are the indicators.
explanation.definitionFit: Labour in childbirth ends in deliveries, so births are its outcome; the question mark flags the pun.

clue.text: Warmly greet runners beginning to finish

indicators.note: the beginning of the word goes to its finish, so the opening letter of the synonym is shifted to the end

parts.note: skis are runners, sliding along snow

explanation.surface: Athletes are greeted warmly as they start for the finish line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to finish' moves the first letter S of SKIS to the end. 'runners' looks like athletes, but means skis.
explanation.definitionFit: A kiss is an affectionate greeting, so to give one is to greet someone warmly.

clue.text: Revered MP deviously ends stalemate involving Queen

indicators.note: to involve is to wrap in, so the shuffled letters enclose another
done by a roundabout route, so the letters of ends stalemate are twisted into a new order

parts.note: R is short for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A respected politician cunningly breaks a deadlock with the monarch's help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deviously' rearranges ENDS STALEMATE; 'involving' puts R among those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An elder statesman is a veteran politician held in high regard for long experience.

clue.text: Stand on which soldiers march according to at least one commander

definitions.meaning: to put up with or tolerate something

definitions.text: on which soldiers march according to at least one commander
definitions.meaning: Napoleon is credited with saying an army marches on its belly

explanation.surface: A platform beneath marching troops, as one general would have it.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means tolerate, and as a noun it is the belly an army proverbially marches on.

clue.text: In pickle, church replaces first of priests in SW London area

indicators.note: one thing takes the place of another, so church comes in where the first of priests was

parts.note: Putney is a district of south-west London on the Thames
first of priests is its initial letter

explanation.surface: Within a sauce, a church takes over from the clergy's leading member in a London suburb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first of priests' is P, the letter swapped out of PUTNEY for CH. PUTNEY is a riverside district in south-west London.
explanation.definitionFit: Chutney is a spiced fruit relish, a type of pickle served with cheese or curry.

clue.text: Big Aussie retiring to outskirts of Rugby remains there

parts.note: OS stands for outsize, a clothing size for the large

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the word for an Australian is read backwards

parts.note: AUS is short for Australian

indicators.note: the outskirts are the edges, so take the first and last letters of Rugby

explanation.surface: A large Australian heads off to the edge of Rugby, a town in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retiring' turns AUS into SUA; 'outskirts of' gives RY. The definition is cryptic: 'remains there' means the bones lie in it.
explanation.definitionFit: An ossuary is a vault or container where the bones of the dead are kept, so human remains rest in it.

clue.text: Win time for convict, once

parts.note: to win something is to attain it

explanation.surface: A prisoner is granted extra time, back in the old days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'once' marks the definition as archaic: attaint was a legal term for convicting and stripping someone of civil rights.
explanation.definitionFit: In old law, to attaint was to condemn someone of a capital crime, so it is an archaic word for convict.

clue.text: Dim, rather goofy working girl transformed by her?

indicators.note: working means in motion or being manipulated, so the letters of the fodder are rearranged

explanation.surface: A silly, slow-witted servant girl is changed by a mysterious woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' looks like part of 'working girl' but rearranges DIM RATHER GOOFY. The girl is Cinderella, the drudge transformed for the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: In the pantomime tale, a magical godmother turns the drudge Cinderella into a princess-like guest.

clue.text: Old queen was idle

parts.note: someone idle did nothing: did, plus O for nothing
O is the round figure zero, meaning nothing

explanation.surface: A former monarch spent her days doing nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'was idle' is read as 'did nothing', with O standing for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Dido was the legendary queen of Carthage, loved and abandoned by Aeneas.

clue.text: British cutting through soft Polish instrument

indicators.note: to cut through is to split open, so British goes into the middle of the word for through

parts.note: via means by way of, or through
P is piano, the musical marking for soft
to hone is to sharpen or polish

explanation.surface: A British person slices through soft Polish goods for a musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' looks like a nationality but is the verb meaning to sharpen; 'cutting' is the insertion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A vibraphone is a percussion instrument with metal bars and motor-driven resonators.

clue.text: Note cheesy material has been sent back

indicators.note: sent back means returned the way it came, so the word for the curdling agent runs backwards

parts.note: rennet is the enzyme used to curdle milk in cheese-making

explanation.surface: A note says a cheese-making ingredient has been returned to sender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent back' reverses RENNET. A TENNER is a British ten-pound note.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenner is a ten-pound banknote, so it is a note of money.

clue.text: Hand over hat daughter's left for potential witness

parts.note: to pass something is to hand it over

indicators.note: has left means gone away, so the letter for daughter is taken out of the hat

parts.note: a derby is a bowler hat
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: Someone is told to hand over a hat after the daughter has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' removes D from DERBY to give ERBY. 'daughter's' reads as 'daughter has'.
explanation.definitionFit: A passer-by happens to be on the spot when something occurs, so may be called on to testify.

clue.text: English medic in residence finally seeks compensation

indicators.note: in places the English medic inside the abbreviation for residence

parts.note: DR is short for doctor

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of seeks

explanation.surface: An English doctor living in at last asks for damages.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a live-in doctor claiming damages; 'in' and 'finally' are the working words.
explanation.definitionFit: Redress is the setting right of a wrong, especially money paid in reparation.

clue.text: Fashion model promises to pay for sweet

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape or make, so the letters of model are made into a new form

parts.note: IOUs are written promises to pay a debt

explanation.surface: A fashion model pledges to pay for a dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion' rearranges MODEL to MELOD. 'sweet' is not a dessert but sweet-sounding.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet can describe music pleasant to hear, which is what melodious means.

clue.text: Are tax rises squeezing new restaurant?

indicators.note: to squeeze is to press in, so the reversed letters close around the abbreviation for new
in a down clue rising means reading upwards, so are and the tax are turned round

parts.note: VAT is value added tax

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether tax increases are crushing a newly opened eatery.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'rises' reads upwards, giving TAVERA; 'squeezing' then grips the new letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A taverna is a small Greek restaurant or tavern.

clue.text: Score with second hook, bagging runs

indicators.note: to bag is to capture and hold, so the outer letters enclose runs

parts.note: a hook is a catch, the fastening on a door
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A cricketer scores with a hook shot in the second over and picks up runs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bagging' puts R inside SCATCH. The surface is cricket: a hook is a batting stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: To score is to scratch a mark onto a surface, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Ulster nurse occupies locked building

parts.note: NI is Northern Ireland, often called Ulster

indicators.note: to occupy is to fill a space, so the nurse goes inside the word for locked

parts.note: shut means closed or locked
SEN is a State Enrolled Nurse, an old British nursing grade

explanation.surface: A nurse from Northern Ireland is inside a locked building.
explanation.walkthrough: SEN was a British nursing qualification, the State Enrolled Nurse; 'occupies' is the insertion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A Nissen hut is a prefabricated semicircular corrugated-iron building, used by the military.

clue.text: In mess, feast doesn't start without politician

indicators.note: without means outside, so the trimmed feast is placed around the politician
the word loses its first letter

parts.note: a junket is a lavish feast or jolly
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: At an army mess, a banquet fails to begin because a politician is absent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside, not lacking; 'doesn't start' trims the feast to UNKET.
explanation.definitionFit: Unkempt hair or clothes are untidy, so the person is in a mess.

clue.text: Want expert to ring playwright missing opening

indicators.note: to ring is to encircle, so the word for expert goes round the trimmed name

parts.note: an ace is an expert

indicators.note: the opening letter of the name is dropped

parts.note: Henrik Ibsen was a Norwegian dramatist

explanation.surface: Someone wants an expert to phone a playwright who missed his premiere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to ring' means to encircle, not to telephone; 'missing opening' drops the dramatist's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Want as a noun means lack, so it is a synonym for a lack or absence of something.

clue.text: Defer insurance protecting a railway crossing river

indicators.note: to protect is to surround and shield, so insurance wraps round the rest

parts.note: cover is insurance protection

indicators.note: the railway crosses the river by stretching across it, so the letters go around it

explanation.surface: Someone postpones insurance for a railway bridge over a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crossing' makes RRY, the railway spanning the river; 'protecting' wraps the insurance round everything.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry over is to postpone something to a later time or account, which is to defer it.

clue.text: Someone close to me put out last of soap

indicators.note: the last letter of the soap's name is put out, or removed

parts.note: Neighbours is a long-running Australian TV soap opera

explanation.surface: Someone dear to me ditched the last of the soap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put out last of' drops the S from NEIGHBOURS, an Australian soap popular in Britain. 'soap' looks like the stuff you wash with.
explanation.definitionFit: The person living next door is near you, so they are someone close to you.

clue.text: Do some Muslims welcome female Anglicans?

indicators.note: to welcome is to take in, so the Muslim word holds the abbreviation for female

parts.note: a Sufi is a member of a mystical Muslim order
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether certain Muslims welcome Anglican women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' as in 'that will do'; 'welcome' is the insertion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To do in the sense of 'that will do' means to be enough, a synonym for be adequate.

clue.text: Fabulous creature's college business service

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', so the definition reads 'fabulous creature is'

parts.note: uni is short for university
CO is short for company
RN is the Royal Navy, one of the armed services

explanation.surface: A mythical beast's university provides a corporate service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabulous' means legendary, from fable, not wonderful.
explanation.definitionFit: A unicorn is a horse with a single horn from myth and legend, a beast of fable.

clue.text: Mountainous country with soldiers and gunmen

parts.note: and means with or plus
OR is other ranks, ordinary soldiers
RA is the Royal Artillery, the gunners

explanation.surface: A Pyrenean country with infantry and artillery.
explanation.walkthrough: OR (other ranks) and RA (Royal Artillery) are British army abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: Andorra is a small country high in the Pyrenees between France and Spain.

clue.text: Rhetorical expressions used about superior groups of players

indicators.note: about means around, so the figures of speech go round the letter for superior

parts.note: tropes are figures of speech
U means upper class or superior, as in U and non-U

explanation.surface: Figures of speech are used about fine bands of performers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts U inside TROPES. U is British slang for upper class.
explanation.definitionFit: Troupes are companies of actors or performers, so they are groups of players.

clue.text: Restyle novel in a pithy way

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters of restyle take a new form

explanation.surface: Someone reworks a novel so it reads more concisely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book but is the anagram signal for RESTYLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Terse means brief and to the point, so the adverb is concisely or pithily.
